claims.text: Rapid-reduction synthesis produces sub-10 nm HEA nanoparticles containing Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, and Cu.
Annealing these nanoparticles at 300°C for 2 hours under an inert atmosphere induces controlled short-range atomic ordering.
Annealing-induced short-range ordering creates and stabilizes specific catalytic active sites.
Short-range atomic ordering tailors adsorbate binding energies.
Tailored adsorbate binding energies improve catalytic performance relative to rapidly quenched, disordered nanoparticles.
The proposed performance improvement depends on minimizing annealing-induced sintering.
The structural mediator consists of moderate short-range order, including altered local coordination environments or surface atomic clusters.
EXAFS and high-resolution TEM can verify the proposed local ordering and lattice rearrangements.
Annealing-induced atomic rearrangements lower the formation energy of active sites such as step edges and defect sites.
Modification of electronic states is the mechanism by which local rearrangements lower active-site formation energies.
Tailored local order optimizes the binding energies of catalytic reaction intermediates.
Optimized intermediate binding energies enhance catalytic turnover.
If particle-size distributions remain unchanged, the proposed catalytic enhancement is independent of size changes.
Annealed nanoparticles will have a lower onset potential or higher turnover frequency for reactions such as oxygen reduction or CO oxidation than unannealed nanoparticles.
Catalytic improvement will correlate with spectroscopic indicators of increased local atomic ordering.
Rapidly quenched, unannealed nanoparticles retain a higher degree of chemical disorder than annealed nanoparticles.
The hypothesis is limited to sub-10 nm Pt-Pd-Au-Ag-Cu HEA nanoparticles made by rapid-reduction chemistry and annealed at approximately 300°C for 2 hours under inert atmosphere.
Annealing may cause partial sintering or morphology changes that independently affect catalytic performance.
The contributions of ordered active sites and particle-size effects may not be quantitatively separable using the proposed experiment alone.
